title: Compton
name: Compton
metaDescription: Compton 1031 exchange advisory for owners of Alameda Corridor-adjacent industrial buildings and value-add apartment properties, including Opportunity Zone tracts.

sections.html: Compton's industrial base runs along the Alameda Corridor, the freight rail line connecting the ports to downtown Los Angeles rail yards, and that corridor has shaped land use in the city for decades. An owner selling in Compton is usually holding a smaller industrial building or an older apartment property, and both categories trade at a scale that keeps the replacement search realistic rather than competing against institutional-size deals elsewhere in the county. Smaller deal sizes here also mean private and first-time exchange buyers make up a larger share of the buyer pool than they would for a larger institutional-scale property elsewhere in the county.

sections.heading: Legacy Industrial Along a Working Rail Corridor
sections.html:
Buildings sitting near the Alameda Corridor benefit from freight rail access that is difficult to replicate elsewhere, even when the buildings themselves are older and smaller than what a modern logistics tenant would prefer. That gives Compton industrial a durable base of demand from tenants willing to trade newer construction for rail proximity.

Multifamily in Compton skews toward smaller, older buildings, many built well before current rent-cap rules existed, and value-add buyers are drawn to the category because rents in a fair number of these buildings still sit below what nearby submarkets are achieving on comparable unit mixes.

sections.heading: What a Compton Owner Is Typically Comparing
sections.html:
Given the deal sizes common here, a Compton identification list generally draws from:

  • Smaller industrial buildings along the Alameda Corridor
  • Value-add apartment buildings built before current rent-cap rules
  • Owner-user light manufacturing space
  • Retail parcels serving surrounding residential neighborhoods
  • DST interests for owners who prefer to exit active property management entirely

sections.heading: Rent-Cap Exposure and Opportunity Zone Considerations
sections.html:
California's statewide AB 1482 rent cap applies to most Compton apartment buildings that are not otherwise exempt, and a value-add buyer's underwriting should reflect that cap rather than assume rents can be pushed to market rate on the timeline a straight comparable-sales analysis might suggest. A lender will expect to see that cap reflected in the pro forma before finalizing terms.

Several census tracts within Compton are designated federal Opportunity Zones, and an owner considering a 1031 exchange alongside Opportunity Zone treatment should have their tax advisor confirm how the two programs interact for the specific property, since the rules for each are separate and combining them requires careful structuring.

sections.heading: Sizing an Identification List for Smaller Deals
sections.html: An owner exchanging out of a smaller Compton apartment building can often stay within the three-property rule if the search stays in the same value-add category nearby. Someone exiting Alameda Corridor industrial and open to a wider mix that includes retail or a different asset class typically needs the 200 percent rule, since a narrow three-property list rarely captures enough comparable range across those categories before the forty-five day deadline.

sections.heading: Budgeting a Compton Value-Add Purchase Line by Line
sections.html:
A numbers-first budget for a Compton value-add apartment building should treat capital improvement costs as the primary underwriting driver rather than a secondary item, since the spread between current in-place rents and market rent only gets captured after unit renovations, and the pace of that capture is limited by the statewide rent cap on any occupied unit. A buyer should model renovation costs unit by unit against realistic turnover timing rather than assuming the whole building can be repositioned in a single year.

Lifecycle cost on older Alameda Corridor-adjacent industrial buildings should account for rail-spur maintenance obligations where a spur is present, along with a standard roof and dock-equipment reserve, since smaller industrial buildings in this pocket of the county are often older than their asking price alone would suggest. A buyer should also confirm current permit status on any outdoor storage or paving use, since older Compton industrial parcels sometimes carry uses that predate current permitting requirements. Given the smaller deal size typical here, an owner should also confirm that title and escrow fees, which do not always scale down proportionally with purchase price, are budgeted as a real percentage of the deal rather than assumed to be a rounding error. A buyer working with smaller purchase amounts should confirm these fixed-cost items early, since they can meaningfully affect the net proceeds available for a follow-on identification if the exchange involves more than one replacement property.

faqs.q: Why do older industrial buildings along the Alameda Corridor still hold demand?
faqs.a: Freight rail access along that corridor is difficult to replicate on a new parcel, so tenants willing to trade newer construction for rail proximity keep demand steady even for older, smaller buildings.

faqs.q: Does the statewide rent cap affect underwriting on a Compton value-add apartment deal?
faqs.a: Yes. AB 1482 applies to most buildings that are not otherwise exempt, and a buyer's pro forma should reflect that cap rather than assume rents can be pushed to market rate on an unrestricted timeline.

faqs.q: Can I combine a 1031 exchange with Opportunity Zone treatment on a Compton property?
faqs.a: The two programs have separate rules, and combining them requires careful structuring. An owner should have their tax advisor confirm how both apply to the specific property before assuming they can be layered together.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange Los Angeles confirm my Compton property qualifies for an exchange?
faqs.a: No. This service coordinates planning, property identification, and communication among an investor's advisors. Whether a specific transaction and property qualify is a determination made by the investor's CPA, tax attorney, and qualified intermediary.
